4.8  Peak‑demand and EMS impact
The billing-demand result is evaluated using apparent 
power in Eq. (33). The grid-only case has a maximum 
demand of 1080  kVA. The existing 930  kW PV case 
reduces this only to 1000  kVA because PV generation 
does not always coincide with the monthly billing peak. After BESS, DSM and EMS coordination, the optimized 
HRES reduces the peak demand to 695 kVA.

HRES reduces the peak demand to 695 kVA. This corresponds to a 35.6% reduction compared with the grid-only

for Shivaji University because maximum demand directly

4.13  Discussion of major research outcomes
The first major outcome is that the existing 930 kW PV 
system already provides a measurable and substantial energy-saving contribution. It reduces annual grid 
import by 1220 MWh and avoids about 1000 tCO2 per 
year. This confirms that rooftop PV is a technically suitable first-stage renewable-energy measure for the campus. The second major outcome is that the campus still 
has significant additional renewable-integration potential.

section: 7.	 The numerical results are translated into a phased
paper_title: From conventional campus grid to optimized HRES microgrid: a grid-constrained techno-economic and environmental assessment of renewable energy integration at Shivaji University, India
text:
enewable-energy measure for the campus. The second major outcome is that the campus still 
has significant additional renewable-integration potential. The optimized HRES reduces grid import from 
2430 MWh/year in the existing PV case to 1175 MWh/
year. This additional saving of 1255 MWh/year cannot be 
achieved by PV expansion alone; it requires BESS, DSM 
and EMS coordination. The third major outcome is peak-demand mitigation. The existing PV system reduces peak demand only 
moderately, whereas the optimized HRES reduces peak 
demand from 1080 kVA to 695 kVA. This indicates that 
BESS and DSM are essential for demand-charge reduction and transformer-load management. The fourth major outcome is renewable self-sufficiency. The existing PV system provides a self-sufficiency index 
of 33.4%, while the optimized HRES improves it to 67.8%.

section: 7.	 The numerical results are translated into a phased
paper_title: From conventional campus grid to optimized HRES microgrid: a grid-constrained techno-economic and environmental assessment of renewable energy integration at Shivaji University, India
text:
come is renewable self-sufficiency. The existing PV system provides a self-sufficiency index 
of 33.4%, while the optimized HRES improves it to 67.8%. This means that more than two-thirds of the annual campus electricity demand can be supplied by self-utilized

INR 4.85/kWh indicate that the optimized HRES is economically attractive under present Indian institutional 
tariff conditions. The economics further improve under 
tariff escalation scenarios. The sixth major outcome is the practical roadmap for 
implementation.

4.14  Implications for Indian higher‑education campuses
The proposed CMR-ESAF results have wider implications for Indian higher-education institutions. Many 
Indian campuses have large daytime loads, available 
rooftops, HT supply connections, transformer-level 
distribution systems and increasing electricity bills.

4.15  Summary of results
The MATLAB-based simulation confirms that Shivaji 
University can be systematically transformed from a 
conventional grid-dependent campus into an optimized 
HRES-based microgrid. The existing 930 kW PV system 
reduces annual grid import by 33.4% and avoids about 
1000  tCO2/year.

1.  Introduction 
During the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, many 
people in Türkiye began relocating to rural areas, 
seeking to distance their families from crowded urban 
environments. A significant number chose to 
purchase tiny houses and place them on land located 
near—but not within—village boundaries. However, 
these rural regions often lack electricity and gas 
networks, creating a major challenge for residents. 
The net-zero energy building (nZEB) approach 
presents a promising solution. A net-zero energy

The introduction of large amounts of variable and uncertain generation, such as from solar photovoltaics (PV) and wind, is changing
how power systems are planned and operated (Kroposki et al., 2017). Multiple timescales are affected, from decade-scale capacity planning
(Sullivan et al., 2014), to one-time interconnection procedures (Camm
et al., 2012; Manley and Limon, 2018; Wu et al., 2019), to day-ahead
and intra-day generator scheduling (Denholm et al., 2019), and secondscale control (Muljadi et al., 2012; Gevorgian, 2019). As higher
penetrations are achieved, balancing generation and load during
normal operating conditions and during abnormal events becomes
more dynamic (Fig. 1).

The largest power systems in the world today were designed around
the physics of synchronous generators or, more generally, synchronous

2. Power electronic converters
Advances in semiconductor technology and energy-conversion efficiencies of power electronic converters (PECs) during the last few
decades have resulted in the widespread adoption of PECs at various
levels of the power system. At the consumer level, PECs are generally
deployed in the form of DC-to-DC converters for general electronic
devices, or AC-to-DC converters for laptops, computers, and televisions,
to name a few. Large-scale PECs, such as rectifiers and inverters, are
generally used to control the flow of tens of kilowatts to hundreds of
megawatts (or the reactive power equivalent) of power. At the power
transmission level, PECs typically interface variable and uncertain renewable sources, such as solar PV, with the AC power system, resulting
in an asynchronous generation source.

text:

in an asynchronous generation source. The increased integration of
renewable energy sources into the power system consequently leads to
increased PEC penetration, both from an annual energy and instantaneous perspective. PECs have a wide range of applications, and they can generally be
categorized into the following groups:
• AC-to-DC converters (rectifiers)
• DC-to-AC converters (inverters)
• DC-to-DC converters
• AC-to-AC converters
In this paper, the conversion of interest is DC to AC because the
emphasis is on IBRs, which interface the solar PV DC source with the AC
power system. Therefore, in the following sections, the terminology
relating to PECs, in general, also refers to IBRs.

2.1. Power electronic fundamentals
Central to PECs are semiconductor devices operating in switched
mode. In other words, electronic switches are realized using diodes and
transistors. In addition to diodes and transistors, PECs employ static
devices, including inductors, capacitors, and transformers. An integral
part of each PEC is the control system, which is necessary to achieve the
desired output and efficiency. Fig. 6 shows a diode, which is a two-terminal semiconductor device;
and a transistor, which is a three-terminal semiconductor device.

paper_title: Stability and control of power systems with high penetrations of inverter-based resources_ An accessible review of current knowledge and open questions

and efficiency. Fig. 6 shows a diode, which is a two-terminal semiconductor device;
and a transistor, which is a three-terminal semiconductor device. Unlike
the transistor, whose conduction stage depends on an externally applied
signal at the controlled terminal (gate, G), the diode is a passive
switching element, which means that its conductivity is determined by
the applied voltage and current. The diode allows current to flow in one
direction—from the collector (anode) to the emitter (cathode)—while
blocking current in the opposite direction. When the collector terminal
(C) is at a higher potential than the emitter terminal (E), the switch is
closed and the current flows in the direction indicated by i. This current
flow causes a voltage drop from C to E known as a diode’s forward
voltage drop.

voltage drop. When the reversed voltage is applied, from E to C, the
diode becomes reversed-biased and the switch opens. In addition to
forward voltage drop, other important characteristics of diodes are reverse recovery and reverse voltage. The right side of Fig. 6 shows an insulated gate bipolar junction

(PWM) control signal, with switching frequencies in the kilohertz to

Solar PV inverters are used for both stand-alone and grid-tied systems.

2.2. Basic operation
Solar PV inverters are used for both stand-alone and grid-tied systems. Solar PV panels produce DC power, which must be converted to
AC power to interface with the power system, a process that is accomplished with the inverter. Inverters (or charge controllers, depending on the Solar PV interfacing scheme) commonly incorporate
maximum power point tracking control schemes to achieve optimal
energy production, either directly for the DC-to-AC conversion, or while
charging a battery system. The AC output current generated by the
inverter must have the same frequency and maintain a specified relative
phase with the utility grid AC voltage waveform (60 Hz in the United
States) to accomplish the desired power injection into the power
system.

phase with the utility grid AC voltage waveform (60 Hz in the United
States) to accomplish the desired power injection into the power
system. The topology of the basic, single-phase inverter is based on the fullbridge, high-frequency IGBT module (Fig. 7). This topology consists of
four semiconductor switches: four IGBTs with four diodes in antiparallel, two on each branch. The semiconductors of each branch are
complementary in performance, which means that when one is switched on, the other is switched off, and vice versa. The fraction of time
during which a switch pair is in the on state within one switch cycle is
called a duty cycle, with output voltage of the inverter a function of the
duty cycle. Adjusting the duty cycle in a periodic manner is a control
strategy known as PWM.

loss (Zografos and Ghandhari, 2017). On the other hand, a higher

Initially, the majority of grid connected solar PV inverters were
controlled to inject whatever power was currently available (grid-parallel inverters). However, with improved control schemes and grid
codes, the general class of grid-supporting inverters has grown more
common. Grid-supporting inverters modulate active and reactive power
set points in order to support grid stability. A standard mode of operation for grid supporting operation is open loop droop control based
on the active power-frequency (P-f) and reactive power-voltage (Q-V)
coupling characteristics in AC transmission systems.

3. Power system stability
Power system stability is a large field rich in mathematics and firmly
grounded by the physics of power system devices, in particular SMCs,
which has traditionally focused on three domains of stability: rotor
angle, frequency, and voltage (Kundur et al., 2004). At high instantaneous penetrations, solar IBRs can introduce challenges for the
stable operation of power systems. This section discusses these traditional stability domains as well as the anticipated or identified impacts
from high IBR penetrations by reviewing recent stability research with
high levels of IBRs. Additionally, system strength and fault response are
discussed through the lens of high IBR penetration levels.
3.1.

text:

high levels of IBRs. Additionally, system strength and fault response are
discussed through the lens of high IBR penetration levels.
3.1. Measuring stability
Although it is impossible to fully partition the rotor angle, frequency, or voltage domains from each other, doing so is a standard
practice that readily simplifies the approach in determining stability
and aids in identifying mitigating measures (Kundur et al., 2004). In
this section, we briefly review these three measures of stability, and the
next section discusses how IBRs have been shown to impact these metrics in recent stability studies with high IBR penetrations. Additional
review material is provided and referenced in Appendix A.
3.1.1.

review material is provided and referenced in Appendix A.
3.1.1. Rotor angle
Rotor angle stability is the ability of the connected and synchronized SMCs (or more generally, generation sources) to maintain rotor
angles within stable boundaries following a perturbation, with no
persisting oscillations (Kundur et al., 2004). This measure captures the
general concepts of synchronism within the context of rotating machinery. Every SMC has a rotor angle position that is displaced from the
stator AC voltage waveform depending on the power being exported to
the electric grid. See the discussion in Appendix A.2 and Eq. A.2. Because the power output of the machine is determined by the rotor angle,
this is also known as the power angle.

3.1.2. Frequency
Imbalances between generation from SMCs and load result in deviations from nominal frequency. A decrease in frequency indicates that
generation is insufficient to meet the current load, whereas an increase
in frequency indicates that generation exceeds the load. This allows
such deviations to be used as a metric for load balancing and as a signal
upon which power output could be governed.

utilizes frequency deviations to dictate power sharing and output
among systems incorporating multiple machines. At a specified droop
slope, typically 4%–5%, droop control will trigger a participating SMC
to increase power output following a change in frequency. As a basic

3.2. Studying stability with high IBR penetrations
In assessing the stability of a power system, the impacts of a perturbation (such as a load imbalance or fault) on the key stability partitions of voltage, frequency, and rotor angle are typically analyzed. Depending on the size of the power imbalance and the physical influence on the network, there are two fundamentally different approaches
in stability analysis: small-signal and large-signal stability.

load and power flows are changing continuously as the multitudes of
customers adjust their power needs, with these types of changes being
relatively small with respect to the total system load. Assessing the
stability during these minor fluctuations is accomplished through a
mathematical framework known as small-signal stability (Kundur,
1994; Van Cutsem and Vournas, 2007). Significant power imbalances
can occur because of a physical change in the network, such as a fault or
the sudden loss of a generator. Such large perturbations result in a
change in the mathematical structure of the network and are not readily

3.2.1. Small-signal stability
Small-signal stability is a method of assessing stability under small
load and/or generation variations without any physical change to the
network. Since there are no physical changes to the network, a mathematical model can be formulated in the form of differential algebraic
equations and linearized to assess the stability around a steady-state
operating point. All dynamic elements are cast in the form of first-order
differential equations using the state-space model, whereas the network
is approximated algebraically by neglecting the electromagnetic transients associated with power transmission.

paper_title: Stability and control of power systems with high penetrations of inverter-based resources_ An accessible review of current knowledge and open questions
text:
state-space model, whereas the network
is approximated algebraically by neglecting the electromagnetic transients associated with power transmission. When this model is linearized around a steady-state operating point,
a state matrix can be generated and decomposed into eigenvectors and
a diagonal matrix of eigenvalues—the stability of the system can be
determined by the eigenvalues themselves. Generally, a well-defined
system will have an eigenvalue, or pair, associated with a particular
state variable in the system. Participation analysis can be performed to
identify the interplay between various states. Eigenvalues with a negative real part cause a decaying exponential response that goes to zero
over time, which is a general indicator of stability for the affected state. The rate of decay is proportional to the proximity of the eigenvalue real
part to zero.

Large-signal or transient stability refers to the capability of the power

and/or islanding following a fault or contingency event (Kundur et al.,

The responses of generators to a fault on the grid can either improve
or exacerbate the situation. The fault response of IBRs differs from
SMCs for a variety of reasons, including lower current capabilities,
commanded vs. physics-dictated responses, and variations in manufacturer design (NERC, 2018d; Nimpitiwan et al., 2007).

4. Distributed generation
IBRs differ from centralized SMCs, both in terms of scale as well as
their location on the grid. Whereas most SMCs are connected directly to
the transmission system, a large portion of solar IBRs are connected to
the distribution system as residential rooftop or commercial systems
(Feldman et al., 2020). This distributed generation (DG) is comprised of
many smaller systems rated from just a few to hundreds of kVA, unlike
large transmission-connected assets that are typically tens to hundreds
of MVA (Lin et al., 2017).

paper_title: Stability and control of power systems with high penetrations of inverter-based resources_ An accessible review of current knowledge and open questions

large transmission-connected assets that are typically tens to hundreds
of MVA (Lin et al., 2017). Some IBR plants also fall between these two
clear categories, that is, there are distribution-connected IBR plants
whose larger size and/or ownership structure (i.e., utility-, generation
company-, or community-owned, rather than customer-owned) makes
the “utility-scale” label appropriate despite not being directly connected to the transmission system nor reaching the tens of MVA
threshold (Seguin et al., 2016). Because the distribution system has
historically been an interface between transmission and consumption
(primarily characterized by unidirectional power flow), the presence of
large quantities of DG, as well as utility-scale generation that is distribution connected, can complicate operational practices (Seguin et al.,
2016).

4.1. Impacts of distributed generation
The presence of DG has both positive and negative impacts on the
power system that are generally proportional to the penetration level. A
primary benefit of DG is that the colocation of DG with load reduces
system losses associated with the transmission system (Eftekharnejad
et al., 2013). Further, DG development, in particular on rooftops, does
not require the acquisition of dedicated land for equipment.

5. Simulation and modeling
Bulk power systems are complex, large-scale systems. As a result,
direct experimentation is often not possible, and the field relies heavily
on modeling and simulation for verification and validation of new
ideas. The strategies for simulation and modeling are in a state of
flux–like power systems themselves, which are fundamentally changing
with the rapid growth of new generation technologies such as IBRs. This
section first describes the two major types of simulation used for
studying power system dynamics: RMS and electromagnetic transient
(EMT) simulation. Next, general challenges for meaningful simulation
regardless of type are presented.
5.1. RMS simulation
One common approach for simulating large power systems is to
treat the states of the network (currents and voltages) as steady-state
variables.

text:
lation
One common approach for simulating large power systems is to
treat the states of the network (currents and voltages) as steady-state
variables. In a real power system, voltages and currents are approximately sinusoidal waveforms of a common system frequency. In the
steady-state network approximation, the network states are represented
by a single complex number, typically expressed using phasor notation,
as shown in Fig. 17. The magnitude of the phasor corresponds to the
magnitude of the waveform, and the phase is measured relative to a
reference that is common to the entire network. This simplification
reduces the system to one of algebraic relationships instead of differential equations. When these assumptions are met, an iterative solution
method, such as the Newton-Raphson method, can be employed to
solve for the steady-state load flow.

and dynamic simulations, among other software tools. It is common

In addition to the technical details about the type of simulation
used, there are many practical considerations to ensure useful modeling. In North America, NERC is responsible for developing models
that can be used by industry and researchers. For example, a NERC
working group developed the DER_A modeling framework, which can
be used to model both utility-scale and residential-scale PV far more
effectively than previous attempts (Green, 2019).

and parameterizing the model appropriately, ensuring a common
modeling framework. For models of specific generating plants, regulatory agencies typically rely on models provided by the plant owner. In Australia, concerns
over commercial sensitivity mean that publicly available PSCAD models

The goal of simulation is often to study system behavior during
faults or other abnormal conditions. Unfortunately, these aspects of a
system are often the most complex and most difficult to model. As
discussed previously, RMS-type simulators are often inadequate in
identifying potential causes of tripping, such as short transient overvoltages, reverse current flow, or loss of PLL synchronism (NERC,

PV plant: the power flow will vary from near zero to near maximum on
a daily basis. More generally, the variability of weather dependent renewable sources will lead to additional variance in transmission system
loading. In contrast, power flows in a system dominated by SMCs remain relatively more constant with respect to direction and daily
timescales (Glover and Sarma, 1994).

timescales (Glover and Sarma, 1994). Assessing the large-signal stability of such a system requires the simulation of many credible contingencies but only a small sample of load flow cases. For example, in
(Miller et al., 2014), the stability of the Western Interconnection is
studied only for heavy summer and light spring load flow cases. In a
system with more IBRs, the space of possible load flows is expanded,
and hence more simulations may be required. In Münz and Romeres
(2013), an analytic framework is developed to determine the space of
possible stable power flows to provide a theoretical background and
reduce the computational burden.

text:
6. Conclusion
The traditional approaches to power system operations are undergoing a transformation as IBR penetrations, both by annual energy and
peak instantaneous power, continue to increase in systems all over the
world. While there are no fundamental hindrances to very high penetrations of IBRs in power systems, they do require amended approaches
to ensure proper stability and operation. The forms these changes need
to take are shaped by the physical differences of SMCs and IBRs. SMC
control and stability is based on the massive, rotational characteristics
of generators, whereas IBRs are built up from power electronic
switches. Because modern power systems were formed around SMCs,
our traditional approaches to stability and control assume large quantities of rotational inertia, which IBRs cannot provide.

paper_title: Stability and control of power systems with high penetrations of inverter-based resources_ An accessible review of current knowledge and open questions

our traditional approaches to stability and control assume large quantities of rotational inertia, which IBRs cannot provide. What IBRs can
provide is fast response (generally faster than SMCs); nonetheless this
difference complicates the large scale integration and control of IBRs in
AC power systems. This paper’s discussion of power electronics, IBR control strategies,
and their stability implications reveals significant potential to mitigate
operational challenges with grid supporting IBRs (e.g., fast-frequency
response). Furthermore, research and development of grid forming IBR
technology is progressing rapidly, such that large 100% IBR power
systems, as well as hybrid SMC-IBR systems that experience the full
range of instantaneous IBR penetrations, may be viable options in the
coming decade(s).

rooftop PV systems but consisting also of utility-scale PV connected to
the distribution system, has the benefit of reducing losses, but complicates the operation of distribution systems originally designed for
one-way flow. Many of the resulting voltage issues, as well as bulk level

accurately capture the operation of these IBRs were discussed.

Power grids are complex networks consisting of generators, transmission lines, and consumer loads, all designed and operated to transport energy
from the source to consumer. Connecting any two of these three stages (or the intersection of multiple transmission lines) are points known as buses. These systems are run as alternating current (AC), which transmit real (P) and reactive power (Q). Real power, measured in watts (W), is the power
actually delivered to the loads to perform some type of work (i.e. the power consumers pay for, when delivered over a period of time; a watt-hour
(Wh)).

The frequency of oscillation in the AC power system is electromagnetically linked to the physical rotation of the rotors found in traditional energy
generators, such as coal and nuclear plants. Energy within these generators is harvested through heating pressurised steam and strategically funnelling it to rotate a turbine. This system is called the prime mover. There are typically one or two pole pairs within these turbines that rotate in
synchronous or half-synchronous speeds at 3,600 RPM or 1,800 RPM, respectively, where the number of pole pairs serves to multiple the RPM to the
output frequency.

1 Overview 
At present, power system operations and controls are primarily dictated by and designed for the 
physical characteristics of synchronous machines. The fundamental form and feasible 
functionalities of power systems are rapidly evolving as more inverter-based resources (IBRs) 
are integrated [1]. In this document, the term ‘inverter-based resource’ is used in a general sense 
and is intended to cover plants/assets consisting of one or more inverters connected to 
generation, storage, and transmission/distribution-asset power electronic devices (e.g.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
lants/assets consisting of one or more inverters connected to 
generation, storage, and transmission/distribution-asset power electronic devices (e.g. HVDC 
converters, STATCOMs, etc.). An IBR can be connected anywhere in the power system, 
including transmission, distribution, and customer premises. The individual power electronic 
devices such as inverters and wind turbine generators within an IBR plant are referred to as IBR 
units. To manage the integration of large amounts of IBRs, system planners need accurate IBR 
simulation models to assess their stability and performance under a variety of operating 
conditions. It is, however, challenging to acquire such models for various reasons, and if 
provided, internal control details are often not accessible to the user [2; 3].

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
wever, challenging to acquire such models for various reasons, and if 
provided, internal control details are often not accessible to the user [2; 3]. Increasing use of 
nonlinear and adaptive control, dynamically varying system topology and configuration, and 
wirelessly transmitted software updates to millions of IBRs from scores of manufacturers further 
compound challenges associated with scalable system-level analysis. In addition, performance 
verification and power system stability assurance are needed to ensure proper performance of the 
IBRs under grid operations. Communications and distributed optimization paradigms have been 
proposed as solutions to the challenges highlighted above, but they do not offer options for realtime control and power system stabilization. Furthermore, cybersecurity requirements can 
introduce delays and challenges in this regard.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
ions for realtime control and power system stabilization. Furthermore, cybersecurity requirements can 
introduce delays and challenges in this regard. Existing standards [4; 5] in this broad area are in 
different stages of adoption. At present these standards focus primarily on grid-following (GFL) 
technologies, and thus their requirements are generally not designed to ensure acceptable power 
system operation with grid-forming (GFM) resources. In some cases, those requirements may not 
be appropriate for or may even inadvertently limit the use of GFM resources. Currently, each inverter manufacturer may have a slightly different perception or position 
regarding the notion of GFM and its performance. As a result, for the same event on the 
power grid, there can be variation in response across manufacturers.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
ng the notion of GFM and its performance. As a result, for the same event on the 
power grid, there can be variation in response across manufacturers. This variation results 
in an increased uncertainty in response across the system, which can have undesired 
consequences, as experienced in recent years with existing inverter technology through 
multiple events around the world. To avoid running into a similar situation with a 
widespread adoption of GFM technology, development of performance specifications is 
important as they can help provide guidelines to inverter manufacturers regarding the 
approach to be taken with respect to design and implementation of newer inverter products 
and associated delivery of services. 2

1.1 Grid-Forming (GFM) Controls 
The UNIFI Consortium defines GFM IBR controls as follows in accordance with the North 
American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) [6] definition: 
“GFM IBR controls maintain an internal voltage phasor, i.e., ac voltage magnitude and 
angle, that is constant or nearly constant in the sub-transient to transient time frame.”  
The time frames specified in this section are intended as general descriptions rather than 
requirements or hard limits as sub-transient and transient times are a function of machine 
characteristics.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
nded as general descriptions rather than 
requirements or hard limits as sub-transient and transient times are a function of machine 
characteristics. This definition means that the GFM IBR will nearly immediately (in the subtransient time frame) begin to respond to changes in the external system and attempt to maintain 
IBR control during challenging network conditions to maintain grid stability. In GFM IBRs, the 
voltage phasor is controlled to maintain synchronism with other devices in the grid at steadystate conditions while regulating the active and reactive power appropriately to support the grid.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
synchronism with other devices in the grid at steadystate conditions while regulating the active and reactive power appropriately to support the grid. This contrasts with conventional GFL IBR controls wherein immediately after a disturbance (0-5 
cycles), within the normal operating range of voltage, the output current phasor magnitude and 
angle remain nearly unchanged, and the current phasor begins changing only within the transient 
time frame (tens of cycles) to strictly control the active and reactive power being injected into the 
network. This change in current is the result of the action of outer loop controls within the GFL 
IBR. For a disturbance within the normal operating range of voltage, on the shortest (sub-transient) 
timescales (roughly 0-5 cycles after a disturbance), a conventional (or legacy) GFL inverter’s 
control objective is to maintain its output current.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
timescales (roughly 0-5 cycles after a disturbance), a conventional (or legacy) GFL inverter’s 
control objective is to maintain its output current. Subsequently, in the transient timescale (tens 
of cycles), its objective is to maintain the desired active power and reactive power or change it 
according to a transient setpoint change, e.g. due to frequency-droop operation, so it does not 
maintain a fixed voltage magnitude or phase angle on those timescales. On longer timescales (a 
couple of seconds for conventional/legacy GFL plants and 50 ms to a couple of seconds for new 3

tracking (MPPT), frequency response, and voltage regulation (usually based on commands 
provided by a plant controller). On the other hand, a GFM inverter’s control objective, on the shortest (sub-transient) timescales 
(roughly 0–5 cycles after a disturbance), is to maintain the desired voltage magnitude and phase 
angle and prioritize the support of voltage magnitude and frequency at its terminals. Because of 
its implicit prioritization of attempting to maintain voltage magnitude and phase angle in the subtransient time frame, a GFM inverter does not maintain fixed active or reactive power on those 
timescales.

timescales. On longer timescales, a GFM inverter that is designed to operate on a power system 
with other GFM devices or synchronous machines adjusts its voltage and frequency to 
synchronize with other sources. The primary energy source and IBR rating may limit the capability of the IBR to provide 
capabilities and services. Newer IBR plants with GFL controls can provide fast frequency and voltage response within the 
sub-transient timeframe. As a result, the demarcation line between GFL and GFM can become 
blurred in terms of responses to disturbances and as such, UNIFI recommends the use of 
performance specifications and functional requirements to determine the necessary and required 
operation from IBR plants.

1.2 Scope 
The UNIFI Specifications for GFM IBRs establish functional requirements and performance 
criteria for integrating GFM IBRs into electric power systems at any scale. This may include 
devices used at the local customer, microgrid, distribution, and transmission scales.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
IBRs into electric power systems at any scale. This may include 
devices used at the local customer, microgrid, distribution, and transmission scales. These 
specifications cover all grid-forming technologies applications including, but not limited to 
battery storage, solar photovoltaics (PV), wind turbines, high voltage direct current (HVDC) 
systems, static synchronous compensators (STATCOMs), uninterruptible power supplies (UPS), 
supercapacitors, fuel cells, or other yet-to-be-invented technologies. While each may have 
different dc side and energy limitations, this specification focuses on the ac side performance 
requirements as they relate to interoperability between GFM IBRs and the power system.

text:

requirements as they relate to interoperability between GFM IBRs and the power system. 5

1.3 Purpose 
The purpose of the UNIFI Specifications for Grid-forming Inverter-based Resources is to 
provide uniform technical requirements for the interconnection, integration, and interoperability 
of GFM IBRs of any size in electric power systems of any scale. 
1.4 Limitations 
Local system conditions and scenarios, hardware device limits, and limitations of the source 
behind the IBR (e.g., energy storage state of charge, wind turbine mechanical constraints, nonlinear DC source characteristics) can impact the ability of a GFM resource to meet the 
performance criteria.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
wind turbine mechanical constraints, nonlinear DC source characteristics) can impact the ability of a GFM resource to meet the 
performance criteria. In such situations, detailed studies and assessments should be carried out to 
determine whether and to what extent the performance criteria can be relaxed under a mutual 
agreement with all the parties such as manufacturers, developers, and system planners. Further, 
performance requirements for GFL plants, such as the performance requirements laid out in 
standards such as IEEE 2800-2022 [5], ENTSO-E [8] Requirements for Generators, and IEEE 
1547-2018 [4], generally also apply to GFM IBRs. There are circumstances in which a 
requirement of a standard such as IEEE 1547-2018 or IEEE 2800-2022 is not practical for a 
GFM IBR and exceptions may be warranted until these standards can be updated to fully account 
for GFM inverters.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
EE 2800-2022 is not practical for a 
GFM IBR and exceptions may be warranted until these standards can be updated to fully account 
for GFM inverters. For example, since GFM IBRs are prioritizing voltage response, they may 
not control power as quickly as GFL IBRs. The synchronization-related performance criteria in 
this document do not apply to a GFM IBR that is designed to act as the only grid-forming 
resource in a power system, without the need to synchronize with other GFM sources or other 
power systems. This document specifies GFM capabilities but does not specify the utilization of those 
capabilities. In general, a capability is an inherent property of a device or plant, and its utilization 
refers to how it is operated. See Clause 1.4 of IEEE 2800 for a discussion of capability versus 
utilization.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
a device or plant, and its utilization 
refers to how it is operated. See Clause 1.4 of IEEE 2800 for a discussion of capability versus 
utilization. Constraints on power, energy, and current can impact the utilization of GFM capabilities. For 
example, an operator would need to maintain headroom to ensure a GFM Tier 3 device can meet 
Tier 3 performance expectations at any given moment, but operation of the device or the plant it 
is part of is not in the scope of this document. The capability associated with each GFM Tier is 
an inherent characteristic of the GFM device, but how it is operated is not. In other words, if a 
Tier 3 GFM device is sometimes operated without active power headroom, its GFM performance 
may be limited at those times, but that does not mean the device itself is not in GFM Tier 3.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:

may be limited at those times, but that does not mean the device itself is not in GFM Tier 3. 6

1.5 Constraints Due to Input Source 
Site-specific integration and operation studies should consider the ratings of the GFM IBRs 
utilized. The GFM IBR may specify performance metrics (e.g. the speed and duration of power 
response to disturbance or other parameters) that may be constrained by the basic limitations of 
the DC source. The GFM IBR's input source can influence the performance of the inverter and 
may impact its ability to provide specific grid services. For example, a wind turbine’s speed of 
response to frequency variations in the grid may be slower than a battery energy storage system’s 
speed of response.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
mple, a wind turbine’s speed of 
response to frequency variations in the grid may be slower than a battery energy storage system’s 
speed of response. A GFM IBR’s ability to respond to disturbances depends on both the IBR’s capability and how 
the IBR is operated; specifically, when at or near a power, energy, or current limit, the GFM 
performance may be reduced. This document specifies the IBR’s capability, but it does not 
specify how the IBR should be operated. Because a GFM IBR is required to be dispatchable (per 
section 2.1.2), it should be possible to operate it such that a margin relative to the IBR’s power 
and energy limits is maintained if desired.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
(per 
section 2.1.2), it should be possible to operate it such that a margin relative to the IBR’s power 
and energy limits is maintained if desired. 7

2 Performance Requirements for GFM IBRs 
This section describes performance requirements for GFM resources connected to an electric 
power system based on the GFM tiers described Appendix A. These performance requirements 
are to be provided regardless of the type of GFM resource and the strength of the grid to which it 
is connected. There can be an overlap between some of the expectations listed in this section for 
GFM and the performance expectations of GFL resources.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
connected. There can be an overlap between some of the expectations listed in this section for 
GFM and the performance expectations of GFL resources. As understanding of the applicability 
of GFM technology evolves, different sets of requirements may be established depending on the 
power system type and scale that the GFM IBR is or will be interconnected to. These requirements may not completely apply to GFM inverters that are not intended to parallel

2.1 Performance Requirements for Operation Within Normal Grid 
Operating Conditions 
Normal operations for electric power system locations are defined by operation within a narrow 
range around nominal voltage and frequency (referred to as normal voltage and frequency 
ranges), with the ability to go outside of those ranges for short periods of time (for events such as 
motor starting, step load change, step generation change, and other similar events on the system). Normal operational conditions for a power system are typically given by a standard (e.g., ANSI 
C84.1).

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
ange, and other similar events on the system). Normal operational conditions for a power system are typically given by a standard (e.g., ANSI 
C84.1). To maintain reliable grid operations, it is essential that power system generators be able 
to maintain voltage and frequency within the specified ranges during normal operation and return 
the system to normal operational ranges after an event that would take them outside the ranges.  
2.1.1 Autonomously Support the Grid 
2.1.1.1 Requirements 
GFM IBRs are expected to autonomously respond to changes (both transient and steady state) in 
their locally measured signals (e.g., terminals of IBR or point of interconnection (POI) voltage, 
current, and frequency) to support the local power system per the appropriate GFM performance 
tier.  
2.1.1.2 Comments 
For example, in the transmission network, if an IBR’s locally measured voltage drops, the IBR or 
IBR plant may be expected to increase its reactive power output to help raise the power system 
voltage to a pre-defined scheduled voltage,

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
he IBR or 
IBR plant may be expected to increase its reactive power output to help raise the power system 
voltage to a pre-defined scheduled voltage, regardless of whether it is GFL or GFM. Note that 
there are other allowable operating modes for GFL such as fixed power factor mode. If a grid 
event occurs that leaves a GFM IBR connected to a weak grid (i.e., voltage sensitivity and/or low 
inertia) the GFM IBR should be able to continue to help maintain nominal voltage and frequency 
of the grid, up to the level it can support. The level of support from the GFM IBR plant may be 
related directly to its hardware limitations (e.g., current rating of IBR, energy storage state of 
charge, etc.), or it may be limited by downstream or system side devices such as transformer or 
cable thermal limits external to the IBR or IBR plant itself.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
etc.), or it may be limited by downstream or system side devices such as transformer or 
cable thermal limits external to the IBR or IBR plant itself. This autonomous grid support should 
occur over the sub-transient and transient timescale. Over longer time scales, it is possible the 
plant itself will receive outside communications of new dispatch setpoints or curtailment from a 
system operator working to manage the grid event. 
2.1.2 Dispatchability of Power Output 
2.1.2.1 Requirements 
When operating as part of an interconnected grid, a GFM IBR plant’s steady state power output, 
within the normal range of voltage magnitude and frequency, should be dispatchable either 
through system operator control or by a locally determined goal that may be based upon a market 
clearing solution.

text:

through system operator control or by a locally determined goal that may be based upon a market 
clearing solution. GFM resources in Tiers 1 are not required to have dispatchable active power, 
but shall have dispatchable reactive power. Tier 2 GFM resources may or may not have 10

resources shall have dispatchable active and reactive power capability. 
2.1.2.2 Comments 
For a GFM IBR whose primary input is a variable resource (e.g., wind or solar), it may be set to 
export maximum available output power as determined by wind speed or solar irradiance (unless 
expressly asked by the system operator or local controls to adjust power).

to be changed, it should be possible to do so by remote control. The dispatchability of a GFM 
IBR is determined by the operating point of the GFM IBR and subject to any headroom 
available. Limits of GFM IBR should be understood by the dispatcher.

2.1.3 Provide Positive Damping of Voltage and Frequency Oscillations 
2.1.3.1 Requirements 
It is expected that a GFM IBR will present a non-negative resistance or damping to the grid 
within the frequency range of common grid electrical resonances to prevent the initiation of any 
adverse interactions or oscillations. See Section 6 and Appendix A for details of the applicability 
of this requirement to different GFM tiers and quantified frequency-domain requirements. 
2.1.3.2 Comments 
Specific details on the magnitude of damping are expected to be provided by the system planner 
on a system specific basis.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
ements. 
2.1.3.2 Comments 
Specific details on the magnitude of damping are expected to be provided by the system planner 
on a system specific basis. The GFM IBR should avoid negative damping effects with lowfrequency resonances related to series compensation of transmission lines. GFM IBR should also 
avoid higher frequency resonances due to shunt capacitances or line/cable charging, and 
resonances due to control interactions with GFL IBRs.

power system.1 Exceptions to this requirement may be warranted in circumstances where an 
internal resonance within the IBR coincides with a grid resonance, in which case the IBR may 
prioritize self-protection over providing damping. The GFM IBR is also expected to not

2.1.4 Active and Reactive Power Sharing Across Generation Resources 
2.1.4.1 Requirements 
A GFM IBR is expected to autonomously share power (e.g., incrementally increase or decrease 
power burden within its capability) with other generation resources at all times using the 
principles of droop akin to the operation of conventional synchronous generators or GFL IBRs. IBRs in all GFM Tiers shall share reactive power. For Tier 1 GFM IBRs, only reactive power 
sharing is required.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:

sharing is required. Tier 2 has limited active power sharing capability, and Tiers 3 and 4 have 
full active power sharing capability.   
2.1.4.2 Comments 
As an example, on the transmission system, this property is typically achieved from resources via 
droop on frequency for sharing of active power [9] and droop on voltage for sharing of reactive 
power. It is expected that principles of droop will most likely be employed, at one or more 
timescales, to achieve this autonomous power sharing and supply/load balance. Here, droop is 
not meant to signify the type of GFM control but rather implies the property of interoperation 
that any GFM control type must possess.

not meant to signify the type of GFM control but rather implies the property of interoperation 
that any GFM control type must possess. In other words, this requirement is not meant to imply 
that the GFM control structure known as “droop-based GFM” is required; other control 
structures are permitted as long as a droop output characteristic is presented to the grid. The 
expectation is that the system will achieve a steady-state operating point (potentially offnominal) within the normal operating voltage and frequency ranges while ensuring proper power 
sharing and balance between total supply and total generation, after a disturbance.

procurements.  
2.1.5 Operation in Grids With Low System Strength 
2.1.5.1 Requirements 
A GFM IBR is expected to operate stably when connected to a power system with a low system 
strength, as evaluated in the test described in Section 5.  
2.1.5.2 Comments 
This requirement validates GFM performance at low SCR in a simple test system. Operation in 
the specific system where the IBR will be installed should be evaluated separately. Operating 
below the SCR levels tested in Section 5 should also be possible if the GFM IBR is permitted to 
reduce active power to account for steady state network power flow limitations.

reduce active power to account for steady state network power flow limitations. 12

generators and may not be appropriate as metrics of system strength in systems with high levels

GFL inverters may have operational challenges/constraints in weak systems.

2.1.6 Operation Under System Unbalance 
2.1.6.1 Requirements 
A GFM IBR should not actively oppose or prevent the flow of negative sequence current for 
small levels of voltage unbalance.  
2.1.6.2 Comments 
If the provision of large amounts of negative sequence current introduces stress to equipment, 
reduction or limitation of the magnitude of the current may be allowed after discussion with the 
system operator.

reduction or limitation of the magnitude of the current may be allowed after discussion with the 
system operator. In such a case, a continuous negative sequence current limit may be imposed 
besides the total current limit. Instead of opposing the flow of negative sequence current, a GFM 
IBR should provide negative sequence current within its negative sequence current capability 
and total current capability to facilitate voltage balance. In addition, provision of negative 
sequence current from GFM can help existing protection devices in detection of unbalanced 
faults. Asymmetric inverter protections may need to be updated to allow for negative sequence

2.2 Performance Requirements for Operation Outside Normal 
Conditions 
Abnormal conditions on the electric power system (e.g., temporary and permanent faults, 
oscillations, motor stalls, delayed voltage recovery, generation loss, load loss, blackouts) are 
characterized by voltage and frequency excursions outside of the normal operating ranges. The GFM IBR can trip for abnormal conditions when such tripping is allowed or required by 
IEEE 1547-2018 or IEEE 2800-2022 or other applicable requirements or standards as 
appropriate.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
nditions when such tripping is allowed or required by 
IEEE 1547-2018 or IEEE 2800-2022 or other applicable requirements or standards as 
appropriate. Under abnormal grid conditions, the GFM IBR should perform according to the following 
requirements. 
2.2.1 Voltage Ride-Through Capability 
2.2.1.1 Requirements 
A GFM IBR is expected to ride-through events that result in operations outside normal limits. The ride-through capability should follow applicable standards (e.g. IEEE 1547, IEEE 2800) or 
grid operator requirements. This includes not just voltage ride-through, but also ride through of 
other events specified by the relevant standard or system planner such as voltage phase angle 
jumps,  
2.2.1.2 Comments 
During and immediately after a major grid event, it is recommended that a GFM IBR adhere to 
the following principles, listed in order of priority: 
1.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
uring and immediately after a major grid event, it is recommended that a GFM IBR adhere to 
the following principles, listed in order of priority: 
1. Self-protection: The GFM IBR should be allowed to prevent its current, active power, 
energy or any other critical variable from exceeding—even momentarily—a pre-specified 
maximum capability. 
2. System-wide stability: To the extent possible, provided that the GFM IBR has not yet 
encountered any equipment-related constraints and hence does not need to employ selfprotection, the GFM IBR should retain its grid-forming behavior throughout and 
immediately after the event and operate in a manner agreed-upon between plant owner, 
inverter OEM, and system planner/operator that prioritizes system-wide stability. 
3.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
event and operate in a manner agreed-upon between plant owner, 
inverter OEM, and system planner/operator that prioritizes system-wide stability. 
3. Optimality: To the extent possible, provided that priorities of self-protection and 
system-wide stability are both first met, the GFM IBRs should also adhere to (or return 
to) their desired power and/or reactive power setpoints after a major grid event. 14

2.2.2 Performance During Symmetrical Faults 
2.2.2.1 Requirements 
During symmetrical undervoltage events (e.g. due to faults) and symmetrical overvoltage events, 
a GFM IBR is expected to maintain a balanced internal voltage to the extent possible within its 
physical limits.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
and symmetrical overvoltage events, 
a GFM IBR is expected to maintain a balanced internal voltage to the extent possible within its 
physical limits. The GFM IBR should inject current to oppose the change in voltage.  
2.2.2.2 Comments 
The maximum current injected during faults is defined as the IBR short-term rated current 
(ISRC). The ISRC can be more than the continuous rated current for a time-limited period, but 
without exceeding the IBR’s absolute maximum current capability, to increase the range of 
conditions under which the IBR is able to support voltage and frequency. The GFM IBR data 
sheet should provide a magnitude and duration for ISRC that enables the GFM inverter to 
support protection operations or events like transformer inrush and motor starting. For example, 
an ISRC could be given as “provides 1.5 times full-rated current for 2 s”.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
rations or events like transformer inrush and motor starting. For example, 
an ISRC could be given as “provides 1.5 times full-rated current for 2 s”. This value can also be 
programmable in terms of magnitude and time setting to coordinate with other protection 
devices. This capability might also impact the response of unbalanced faults wherein the current 
on one phase exceeds that of the others (see 2.2.3). The intent is to allow OEMs to provide what 
system operators request. The need for current overload capacity will differ between systems. The purpose of this requirement is to meet the needs of protection elements such as overcurrent, 
distance, and directional elements.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
between systems. The purpose of this requirement is to meet the needs of protection elements such as overcurrent, 
distance, and directional elements. Upon fault clearance, the GFM IBR is expected to support the 
stability of other devices in the post-fault network.  
2.2.3 Performance During Asymmetrical Faults 
2.2.3.1 Requirements 
During asymmetrical faults, a GFM IBR is expected to maintain a balanced voltage to the extent 
possible within its physical limits. This naturally results in the GFM IBR outputting unbalanced 
currents, including negative sequence currents.

2.2.5.1 Requirements 
A GFM IBR is expected to modulate active power as required during and after frequency

changes to aid in frequency recovery and stability. Tier 1 GFM IBRs are excepted from this

2.2.5.2 Comments 
In the sub-transient time frame, the power to be injected is expected to have a similar effect to 
that of resisting frequency change subject to the physical limits of the GFM IBR unit and the 
source behind the GFM IBR.2 This behavior can manifest as a form of fast frequency response 
and can aid in reduction of ROCOF of the network, though it may not fit the specific definition 
of fast frequency response used in some regions. Beyond the sub-transient time frame, the GFM 
IBR is expected to respond to frequency adjustments by internal or external controllers to share 
power (droop) with other resources.

3 Additional GFM Capabilities  
This section describes additional capabilities that may be implemented in coordination with the 
system operator. These considerations will vary from site to site, so they should not be 
considered universal requirements for GFM IBR units or GFM IBR plants. 
3.1 Intentional Islanding 
3.1.1 General 
Intentional islands are parts of electrical power systems that operate separately from the main 
power grid. Examples include islanding of an area in a larger interconnected transmission system 
or formation of a microgrid in the distribution network.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
r grid. Examples include islanding of an area in a larger interconnected transmission system 
or formation of a microgrid in the distribution network. Intentional islanding covers both planned 
and unplanned events.  
3.1.2 Requirements 
A GFM IBR that is designed to maintain an intentional island (i.e. Tier 3 and Tier 4 GFM IBRs) 
is expected to be capable of maintaining stable voltage and frequency when intentional islanding 
occurs.  
3.1.3 Comments 
Not all GFM IBRs within the intentional island may have intentional islanding capability. For 
example, an intentional island could contain Tier 1 or Tier 2 IBRs in addition to the Tier 3 or 
Tier 4 IBR(s) that sustain the island.

3.2.1 General 
GFM IBRs in GFM Tier 4 are designed and programmed to provide black start services. If 
implemented, these black start services should be coordinated with system operators to help in

may be essential in high IBR penetration grids since the black start capability may no longer be 
provided by synchronous machines. Not all GFM IBRs are expected to be able to provide blackstart services since it may require additional hardware, design, and functionalities, and therefore 
implementing black-start capability may incur additional cost and require special coordination

3.2.2 Requirements 
Those GFM IBRs that are designated to provide black start services should be designed to be 
able to: 
1. Start and establish the voltage without an external voltage or frequency reference at the 
ac terminals. 
2. Supply transformer, cold-load, and other inrush current needed within the GFM IBR 
limits. This process is a key step in black start since it may cause significant inrush 
current, especially from transformers and motor loads, which is, in general, more 
challenging when using IBRs than synchronous generators due to lower overcurrent 
capability. To facilitate restoration, it may be useful to soft start loads (i.e., by ramping up 
the output voltage at a programmable rate).

3. Provide a steady voltage reference for GFM and GFL IBRs and other resources to 
synchronize to and facilitate a smooth system restoration including synchronization with 
other restored portions of the grid. Note some GFM IBRs may be configured to 
synchronize their own voltage and phase angle to a primary GFM that is providing the 
voltage waveform for the entire system. 
4. If designed to operate in parallel with other black-start GFM IBRs, it should be able to

3.3 Regulating Voltage Harmonics  
3.3.1 Requirements 
The harmonic distortion of the line-to-neutral voltage waveforms produced by a GFM IBR plant 
should comply with the requirements of the system planner.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
e harmonic distortion of the line-to-neutral voltage waveforms produced by a GFM IBR plant 
should comply with the requirements of the system planner. As a result, a GFM IBR may inject 
harmonic currents at its point of interconnection to aid in reducing the amplitude of voltage 
harmonics induced by other power system components. It is not required that GFM IBRs 
actively mitigate voltage harmonics emanating from the AC grid side.  
3.4 Communications Between System Operator and IBR Plant 
3.4.1 Requirements 
When communications are required between the GFM IBR units or plant and the system 
operator, a cyber-secure communications [12] method should be used. The power system and the 
GFM IBR should continue to function as specified by the system operator when communications 
are delayed or interrupted.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
ed. The power system and the 
GFM IBR should continue to function as specified by the system operator when communications 
are delayed or interrupted. It is expected that signals from the power system operator or an 
aggregator would have an update rate on the order of seconds and represent a secondary control 
signal (primary control being autonomous controls inside the IBR unit) for providing power flow 
set points or other commands. Faster communications may be needed to respond to transient 
conditions. A GFM IBR or IBR plant and associated equipment may also provide signals back to 
the power system operator. Examples of these signals include status signals such as online 
devices, switch states, capacity and headroom, and metered values such as frequency, voltage, or 
power flows.

3.5 Secondary Voltage and Frequency Signal Response 
3.5.1 Requirements 
GFM IBR plants that are expected to participate in secondary control, should be able to receive 
an external signal that enables power flow control from a system operator. This is known as the 
secondary control signal since the IBR unit or IBR plant receives an external signal to adjust 
power output. Once it receives new setpoints, the GFM IBR plant is expected to operate (within 
the GFM IBR's limits) at the new steady state condition within the time specified by the system 
operator.

the GFM IBR's limits) at the new steady state condition within the time specified by the system 
operator. Tier 1 GFM IBRs are not required to be capable of participating in secondary 
frequency control. Tier 2 GFM IBRs may also be excepted from this requirement. 19

4 Modeling and Documentation 
When designing and planning the integration of GFM IBR in power systems it is often helpful to 
be able to accurately model the behavior of the GFM IBR under a wide range of operating 
parameters. The model should accurately represent all operational modes available in the IBR 
and the documentation should describe how to configure the modes and parameters.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
ould accurately represent all operational modes available in the IBR 
and the documentation should describe how to configure the modes and parameters. The 
behavior of the GFM IBR when approaching or encountering physical limits is expected to be 
captured in the manufacturer’s provided and validated electro-magnetic transient (EMT) model 
and phasor-domain transient (PDT) model to allow for accurate simulation of the GFM IBR’s 
response to various events. For example, the EMT model should include fault current shaping 
behavior of the GFM IBR, such as the waveform of current during the fault and its duration if the 
fault current is designed to last only for a short period of time. Because EMT simulations are a primary means of validating GFM performance, the EMT model 
of a GFM IBR should be validated.

compared to hardware test data and shown to match sufficiently. IEEE P2800.2 contains 
hardware test procedures and model validation procedures; these can be leveraged for GFM IBR 
unit model validation. Annex G of IEEE 2800-2022 also includes recommendations for 
modeling IBR plants. 20

In steps 2 and 3, the positive sequence active power of the IBR shall change by at least 0.2 p.u. in 
the direction that opposes the phase jump unless limited by the IBR’s current or power limit. At 
least 90% of the required 0.2 p.u. change in active power shall occur during the first line cycle 
following the phase jump. The change in active power shall be sustained for at least 3 line 
cycles. In steps 4 and 5, any oscillations shall be damped.

This test verifies the IBR’s capability to resist and operate stably during sudden changes in 
voltage magnitude.

5.8.2 Criteria 
Following each voltage step, the positive sequence reactive power of the IBR shall change within

shall occur during the first line cycle following the phase jump. Any oscillations shall be damped.

This section describes methods of assessing GFM capability using frequency-domain tests. Section 6.1 specifies GFM performance criteria, some of which are defined using “dynamic 
droop” frequency scans (as further detailed in 6.2 and Appendix A), and others of which are 
defined based on other types of frequency scans (as further detailed in 6.3). These requirements 
are designed to confirm whether an IBR has the small-signal dynamic characteristics associated 
with GFM capability.

(iii) safe and stable interoperability among various devices, and (iv) dynamic performance 
improvements for the entire bulk system. Previous publications on the topic include [19] and 
[20].

6.3 Voltage Source Behavior 
The unique characteristics of a GFM resource are the fast voltage- and frequency-stabilizing 
response during the short time frame following a grid disturbance, and the ability to act as a near 
ideal voltage source with an internal impedance in these fast timescales—essentially, to allow a 
change of current being injected into the grid such that the change in current aids in the 
maintenance of voltage and frequency at the terminals of the device. This core voltage source 
behavior is important for improving grid strength and mitigating stability problems associated 
with low system strength.

frequency-domain response of an ideal voltage source with a reactor in a desired short time 
frame after a disturbance, as seen from the POI. The frequency-domain response of an ideal 
voltage source with a reactor is then used to define the frequency-domain specifications for 
quantifying the voltage source behavior of GFM resources.

6.3.1 Frequency-Domain Response  
6.3.1.1 Reactive Power Response 
The reactive power response of an ideal voltage source with a reactor can be described in the 
frequency domain by a transfer function from the magnitude of the three-phase voltages at the 
POI, Vm, to the reactive power output of the voltage source with a reactor, Q. This Q/V transfer 
function has the characteristics of a second-order low-pass filter with a negative gain and with 
the corner frequency being the same as the fundamental frequency6.

paper_title: UNIFI Specifications for Grid-Forming Inverter-Based Resources: Version 3
text:
he characteristics of a second-order low-pass filter with a negative gain and with 
the corner frequency being the same as the fundamental frequency6. Moreover, if the steady-state 
gain of the Q/V transfer function in VAR/Volt gain is expressed in p.u./p.u., it will be exactly 
equal to the value of short-circuit ratio (SCR) that the ideal voltage source with a reactor 
represents for the base values used for obtaining the gain in p.u./p.u. The response of the Q/V 
transfer function exhibiting a constant negative gain below the fundamental frequency shows that 
the ideal voltage source with a reactor will dispatch positive reactive power during a voltage 
disturbance that is proportional to the drop in the magnitude of voltages at its terminal.

specified in the frequency domain is by its response of the Q/V transfer function. The parameters 
that can be used to define the transfer function characteristic include:  
• Gain: The gain of Q/V transfer function of an ideal voltage source with a reactor is 
constant or flat at frequencies below the fundamental frequency.

scan of a GFM resource can be evaluated over a smaller frequency range, say, 4 to 40 Hz; 
this range covers the short time frame where the voltage source behavior is expected. Again, the gain of the Q/V transfer function of a GFM resource should be almost constant 
within this specified frequency range.

within this specified frequency range. Moreover, the average gain over this frequency

• Phase: The phase of Q/V transfer function of an ideal voltage source with a reactor is 
around 180o at frequencies below the fundamental frequency.

6.3.1.3 Impedance Response 
Because the impedance of an ideal voltage source with a reactor is the same as that of the 
reactor, i.e., an R-L branch, the voltage source behavior of a GFM resource can also be 
quantified using its frequency-domain positive-sequence impedance response.

quantified using its frequency-domain positive-sequence impedance response. If the impedance 
response of a resource resembles that of an inductor (reactor) in the frequency range of interest, 
then the resource can be exhibiting voltage source behavior.

6.3.2.4 Summary  
Voltage source behavior is the core function expected from GFM resources to improve grid 
strength and support stability of bulk power systems. This section has documented three 
frequency-domain test methods for evaluating the voltage source behavior from GFM resources. 39 
This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Performance metrics are defined for each of the test methods to quantify the voltage source 
behavior.

resource including inverter-based resources (battery/wind/solar power plants, high-voltage DC 
converter stations, STATCOM, etc.) as well as rotating machine–based resources (conventional

A.1 Introduction 
These UNIFI frequency-domain specifications are developed with the intent of helping 
promote/ensure (i) do-no-harm dynamic behavior from a GFM IBR, (ii) robustness of operation, 
(iii) safe and stable interoperability amongst various devices, and (iv) dynamic performance 
improvements for the entire bulk system. While these specifications do help with identifying/characterizing GFM versus GFL behavior, 
they go beyond this single purpose and aim to achieve improved stability and robustness of an 
IBR as it provides various services to the network.

and phase shift of the response of the IBR frequency to an active power oscillation with

Frequency Ranges for Dynamic Droop Specifications 
Dynamics below 0.01 Hz are largely governed by system-level and plant-level controls, and no 
meaningful difference exists between GFM and GFL controls. On the other hand, dynamics 
beyond double line frequency do not significantly contribute to system-wide interaction and 
frequency synchronization of devices. Hence, we restrict our attention to the frequency range of 
0.01 Hz to 40 Hz.

paper_title: Survey on data-driven control and its application in cyber-physical energy systems
text:
1. Introduction 
1.1. Cyber-physical energy systems 
With the accelerated development of information and communica- 
tion technologies, a critical mass of instruments and devices with com- 
munication functions has been widely deployed in power systems to en- 
hance state observability, control responsiveness, and operational ﬂex- 
ibility in the face of increased penetration of renewable generation at 
all voltage levels and the mass roll-out of electriﬁcation plans across 
many end-user sectors. This trend is transforming energy systems into 
cyber-physical energy systems (CPESs). CPESs tightly integrate power-electrical infrastructure (i.e., gener- 
ation, transmission, and distribution) with layers of sensing, commu- 
nication, and computation to enable real-time monitoring, protection, 
and control of smart grids [1] .

paper_title: Survey on data-driven control and its application in cyber-physical energy systems
text:
distribution) with layers of sensing, commu- 
nication, and computation to enable real-time monitoring, protection, 
and control of smart grids [1] . By fusing energy systems with infor- 
mation and control, CPESs endow physical assets with computation,

precise actuation, coordinated decision-making, and autonomous oper- 
ation, thereby leading to promising improvements in safety, resilience, 
and eﬃciency [2] . Despite these advantages, CPESs pose signiﬁcant challenges to con- 
trol design. First, the underlying physical plants are often highly nonlin- 
ear, time-varying, and only partially known.

paper_title: Survey on data-driven control and its application in cyber-physical energy systems
text:
gniﬁcant challenges to con- 
trol design. First, the underlying physical plants are often highly nonlin- 
ear, time-varying, and only partially known. Second, network-induced 
eﬀects —e.g., communication delays, packet losses, and cybersecurity 
threats — further complicate the realization of reliable and eﬃcient 
control [3,4] . Traditional model-based frameworks (e.g., optimal con- 
trol [5] , robust control [6] , and model predictive control (MPC) [7] ) 
rely on accurate ﬁrst-principles or identiﬁed models, hindering their 
deployment across geographically distributed, heterogeneous CPES in- 
frastructures. Consequently, there is a surging interest in data-driven 
control paradigms, which leverage operational data directly to design 
controllers without full reliance on detailed system models.

1.2. Reinforcement learning based data-driven control 
Whereas many data-driven approaches estimate a map from data 
to control inputs oﬄine, reinforcement learning (RL), a powerful tool 
within the family of machine learning, embeds policy learning within 
the closed-loop interaction, allowing an agent to stochastically explore 
and adapt to its environment online [11] .

paper_title: Survey on data-driven control and its application in cyber-physical energy systems
text:
g, embeds policy learning within 
the closed-loop interaction, allowing an agent to stochastically explore 
and adapt to its environment online [11] . By formulating power-system 
control tasks as Markov decision processes (MDPs), RL can discover 
adaptive policies that cope with model uncertainty, unmodeled nonlin- 
earities, and evolving operating conditions [12] . In CPESs, RL-based decision mechanisms have attracted intense in- 
terest as a means to overcome the limitations of ﬁxed, model-based con- 
trollers. For example, RL has been applied to voltage regulation [13–15] , 
state estimation [16–18] , energy management [19] , control of power 
converters [20,21] , and economic dispatch [22] . We refer the readers 
to [23] for more references on RL methods applied to CPESs.

text:
control of power 
converters [20,21] , and economic dispatch [22] . We refer the readers 
to [23] for more references on RL methods applied to CPESs. These 
RL methods have demonstrated the ability to adapt to unforeseen dis- 
turbances and networked interactions that hamper traditional control 
laws, thus representing a powerful complement to model-based designs 
in large-scale, uncertain CPES environments. 
1.3. Willems et al.’s fundamental lemma and direct data-driven control 
Despite the early successes of RL in CPESs, its reliance on large 
amounts of data, signiﬁcant computational resources, and the absence of 
formal stability guarantees limit its deployment in safety-critical infras- 
tructure. In parallel, another data-driven frontier has recently emerged, 
founded on Willems et al.’s fundamental lemma [24] .

paper_title: Survey on data-driven control and its application in cyber-physical energy systems
text:
fety-critical infras- 
tructure. In parallel, another data-driven frontier has recently emerged, 
founded on Willems et al.’s fundamental lemma [24] . This result shows 
that, for a controllable linear time-invariant (LTI) system, a single suf- 
ﬁciently rich input-output trajectory spans the entire system behavior 
via linear combinations of its time-shifts. In eﬀect, one can represent 
all admissible future trajectories with a nonparametric, trajectory-based 
formulation. Inspired by this work, a number of applications and generaliza- 
tions have been developed, including state-feedback and robust control 
[25–29] , data-driven MPC [30–33] , nonlinear system control [34,35] , 
and data-driven state estimation [36–38] .

text:

[25–29] , data-driven MPC [30–33] , nonlinear system control [34,35] , 
and data-driven state estimation [36–38] . Although these techniques are 
still maturing, early applications in CPES contexts —such as data-driven 
voltage regulation, fault detection, and grid synchronization —are al- 
ready emerging [37,39,40] . By circumventing explicit system identi- 
ﬁcation, the fundamental lemma framework promises scalable, theo- 
retically grounded solutions to the high-dimensional, uncertain, and 
network-induced complexities of modern CPESs. 
1.4. Outline of this survey 
The remainder of this survey is organized as follows. Section 6 re- 
views a widely used deep reinforcement learning(DRL) framework.
