text:
nitude of 0.3 pu and a grid impedance of 0.04 pu. For the dq-axes
currents, the actual (blue) and the reference values (red) are visualized.
to occur. From Fig. 5, it can be observed that the PCC
voltage is being highly supported inherently by the gridforming structure without any control modiﬁcation during the
fault. Even though this is a particularly attractive feature, this
voltage support is realized through a large injection of reactive
current with a magnitude of 6.7 pu. As the SPC is a voltage-controlled structure, it simply
requests a current reference to maintain the reference voltage
in order to satisfy the demands from the outer PLC and
RPC. Hence, compared to a grid-following converter, the SPC
behaves as a voltage source with controlled amplitude and
frequency.

paper_title: Current Limiting Control With Enhanced Dynamics of Grid-Forming Converters During Fault Conditions
text:
rom the outer PLC and
RPC. Hence, compared to a grid-following converter, the SPC
behaves as a voltage source with controlled amplitude and
frequency. In case of short-circuit fault conditions, the controlled voltage source will naturally respond by injecting very
high current values to sustain its voltage level. With that,
since voltage-source converters (VSCs) must be protected from
overcurrent of the semiconductor devices, the current reference
must be restricted given it is higher than permitted. Even though the SPC can provide grid-supporting functionalities, provided that a power reserve is available, which
enhances the transient stability of the network, the synchronization stability of the converter may be diminished in case

IV. ENHANCED FAULT RIDE-THROUGH OF
GRID-FORMING CONVERTER
Based on the analysis and approaches just described for
current limitation, a method is proposed which limits the
converter current while keeping the fundamental structure of
the grid-forming control during the fault. This is done by combining the two approaches from Section III, i.e., inner current
limitation and outer power reference adjustment. In addition,
a dynamic virtual damping controller is proposed to enhance
the fault recovery process of the grid-forming converter when
the fault is cleared. A. Current Limitation and Reference Power Adjustment
Considering that it is just desired to limit the converter
currents and not anything else during the fault, the current
reference is still the most logical location to intervene.

to provide precise current limitation alongside realizing that

C. Method Comparison and Weak-Grid Performance
With the fault-mode controller and dynamic damping structure being presented, the proposed SPC is compared to the
solution proposed in [22], which represents a comprehensive
and implementable fault-mode controller for a grid-forming
converter during fault conditions. Here, the control structure
is switched to a grid-following PLL-synchronized structure
during the fault to limit the converter currents. When the fault
has been cleared, the transitioning back to the grid-forming
controller is performed using a feedback tracking controller,
which after the fault, aligns the phase-angles of the two
controllers and perform a seamless switching when aligned.

paper_title: Current Limiting Control With Enhanced Dynamics of Grid-Forming Converters During Fault Conditions
text:
VI. CONCLUSION
Grid-forming converters are becoming increasingly attractive as potential candidates for converter control of future
power electronics-based power systems due to their gridfriendly functionalities. As the converter include currentsensitive semiconductor devices, it cannot sustain the behavior
of a voltage source during grid faults as its short-circuit
capability is much lower than that of a synchronous generator. This article discusses the issues of current limitation of
grid-forming converters and introduces a proposed method,
which includes several advantageous properties: instantaneous
limitation of the converter currents, compliance with grid code
requirements, and circumvention to switch the fundamentals
of the control structure during the fault. To that end, enhanced
fault recovery is attained by a proposed dynamic virtual
damping controller. With this, it is shown that the grid-forming
converter can provide grid-supporting functionalities during
normal operating conditions and by only modifying the outer
power reference generation instead of the inner structure, fault
ride-through capability is achieved. The proposed fault mode
and dynamic virtual damping controller of the grid-forming
converter are tested during very weak-grid conditions and its
performance is veriﬁed experimentally.

I. INTRODUCTION 
ITH the rapid development of new energy sources 
such as wind power, photovoltaics (PV), and energy 
storage, renewable energy generation systems 
connected to the grid through power electronic converters 
have advanced significantly [1], [2]. However, as the 
proportion of renewable energy and the installed capacity of 
converters increase, the strength of the power system weakens, 
leading to a low short-circuit ratio (SCR) at the point of 
common coupling (PCC) [3]. Under such weak or ultra-weak 
grid conditions, the grid-forming energy storage converter 
(GFM-ESC) has attracted increasing attention due to the 
voltage and frequency support capabilities [4]-[6]. The GFM-ESC is commonly applied in bidirectional power 
transfer applications, where the converter must deliver power 
to the grid in discharging mode and absorb power from the 
grid in charging mode [7], [8].

nsfer applications, where the converter must deliver power 
to the grid in discharging mode and absorb power from the 
grid in charging mode [7], [8]. In such scenarios, the GFM-
ESC is required to operate reliably at both positive and 
 
 
 
negative rated power under various grid conditions and to 
transition smoothly between discharging and charging modes 
[9]. Although many studies have concluded that the GFM-
ESC does not exhibit stability issues under weak grid 
conditions, limited power transfer capability is often observed 
in practice. This limitation leads to reduced utilization of the 
converter capacity and presents a significant barrier to an 
effective integration of GFM-ESCs into the power systems 
dominated by power electronic interfaces.

effective integration of GFM-ESCs into the power systems 
dominated by power electronic interfaces. The issue of power transfer limits for converters include the 
static power transfer limit (SPTL) [10] and the dynamic power 
transfer limit (DPTL) [11]. SPTL is obtained by solving 
algebraic equations of the physical circuit and requires the 
existence of a steady-state operating point. DPTL, based on 
SPTL, accounts for control system dynamics and is derived by 
solving differential equations that describe both the physical 
circuit and control dynamics. Relevant studies have explored 
the power transfer limitations of converters and achieved 
notable progress.

the power transfer limitations of converters and achieved 
notable progress. The SPTL associated with AC system 
strength in VSC-HVDC systems was analyzed in [12], where 
limited converter apparent power was shown to impose 
additional constraints, requiring a higher minimum SCR. Moreover, the SPTL can be alleviated by providing 
supplementary reactive power support at the PCC [13]. Similarly, [14] demonstrated that the SPTL of a photovoltaic 
plant can be maximized by injecting reactive power until the 
PCC voltage reaches its upper limit. However, the above 
analyses of the SPTL are subject to certain limitations. In 
particular, the systems investigated in [12]-[14] are modeled 
as PQ nodes, which is not consistent with the PV-node 
characteristics inherent to GFM-ESCs.

as PQ nodes, which is not consistent with the PV-node 
characteristics inherent to GFM-ESCs. In addition, the studies 
in [13] and [14] focus exclusively on unidirectional power 
transfer scenarios. As a result, their conclusions do not fully 
extend to GFM-ESCs operating under bidirectional power 
transfer conditions. Since the SPTL only considers circuit power flow and 
converter capacity constraints, it does not reflect the impact of 
control dynamics. Therefore, the DPTL, incorporating the 
dynamic behavior of converters, has attracted significant 
research interest.

interaction between the PLL and current loop, [16] examined 
the PLL and power loop, and [17] presented a comprehensive 
model including all control dynamics. Despite the modeling 
differences, these works consistently identified the PLL-

strong grid scenarios, particularly addressing small-signal 
stability issues [23]-[25]. Only a limited number of studies 
have explored control strategies to enhance the power transfer 
capability of converters under weak grid conditions. In [13], 
the reactive power loop is modified from conventional droop 
control to VSG control, which improves the power transfer 
capability under weak grids. Nevertheless, the results of this 
paper indicate that even with VSG control, insufficient power 
transfer capability can still occur under extremely weak grid 
conditions (SCR=1). In [14], a voltage compensation term is 
introduced into the reactive power loop to increase reactive 
current injection, thereby enhancing the power transfer 
capability of grid-following converters under weak grids.

current injection, thereby enhancing the power transfer 
capability of grid-following converters under weak grids. However, this approach is only applicable to photovoltaic 
inverters and does not extend to GFM-ESCs operating in 
charging mode. In fact, when applied to the charging operation 
of a GFM-ESC, this method may further deteriorate the power 
transfer capability. In contrast to GFL-ESCs, where the operating point remains 
essentially fixed once a power reference is set, the operating 
point of a GFM-ESC can vary significantly with grid 
impedance and control strategy, even under the same power 
reference. This results in DPTL in GFM-ESCs that are not 
primarily caused by small-signal instability, but rather by 
changes in operating points due to control dynamics and 
parameter settings.

primarily caused by small-signal instability, but rather by 
changes in operating points due to control dynamics and 
parameter settings. Notably, fluctuations in PCC voltage and 
reactive power have a critical impact on the power transfer 
capability of GFM-ESC. Furthermore, most current studies on 
DPTL for energy storage converters focus on the discharging 
operation, while the charging mode remains largely 
unexplored. To address the above research gaps, this paper focuses on 
the GFM-ESC, providing a comprehensive analysis of SPTL 
characteristics under different grid strengths in both 
discharging and charging modes, as well as DPTL 
characteristics under various parameter configurations of the 
reactive power loop and virtual impedance.

reactive power loop and virtual impedance. Furthermore, an 
improved strategy is proposed to effectively overcome power 
transfer difficulties under ultra-weak grids, thereby enhancing 
the capacity utilization and adaptability of GFM-ESC. To 
conclude, the main contributions and innovations of this paper 
are as follows. 
1) It reveals that the SPTL of the GFM-ESC exhibits 
asymmetry between discharging and charging modes, 
with the root cause identified as grid resistance. This 
asymmetry becomes more critical under weak grid 
conditions with high R/X ratios, where stable operation at 
rated charging power may not be achievable.

conditions with high R/X ratios, where stable operation at 
rated charging power may not be achievable. As a result, 
power transfer limitations during charging mode under 
ultra-weak grids can lead to instability and underutilization of the converter capacity. 
2) A third-order nonlinear dynamic model is developed, and 
a phase trajectory method is utilized to characterize the 
DPTL of GFM-ESC.

2) A third-order nonlinear dynamic model is developed, and 
a phase trajectory method is utilized to characterize the 
DPTL of GFM-ESC. The analysis reveals that, even with 
the presence of the SPTL, insufficient voltage support 
due to the voltage regulation coefficient of the reactive 
power loop can prevent the GFM-ESC from achieving 
rated power output and cause issues during power 
transition between positive and negative full power. 
3) To address the instability induced by insufficient DPTL 
under ultra-weak grid conditions, an adaptive voltage 
compensation strategy based on reactive power deviation 
is proposed. This strategy enhances the voltage support 
capability and significantly improves the power transfer 
performance and capacity utilization of the GFM-ESC. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.

II derives mathematical models of the GFM-ESC under both 
constant and variable PCC voltage conditions to analyze SPTL 
across different operation modes and grid strengths. Section 
III establishes nonlinear models and applies a phase trajectorybased method to investigate the DPTL with control dynamics. Section IV presents the adaptive voltage compensation strategy 
based on reactive power deviation to address instability caused 
by insufficient DPTL under ultra-weak grids, along with 
simulation results. Section V provides experimental validation 
for the theoretical analysis and the proposed method. Section 
VI concludes the paper.

section: III. DPTL ANALYSIS OF GFM-ESC UNDER DIFFERENT
text:
III. DPTL ANALYSIS OF GFM-ESC UNDER DIFFERENT 
OPERATING MODES 
The previous section analyzed the SPTL of the GFM-ESC 
in both charging and discharging modes under constant and 
variable PCC voltage conditions. However, the derivations did 
not account for specific control strategies, which can lead to 
the DPTL being lower or even significantly lower than the 
SPTL. To investigate the impact of control strategy on the 
DPTL of the GFM-ESC, this section establishes the nonlinear 
model of the GFM-ESC and employs phase trajectory analysis 
to examine the DPTL. As demonstrated in Section Ⅱ, the PCC 
voltage magnitude directly influences the power transfer 
capability of the GFM-ESC, and this magnitude is regulated 
by the reactive power loop and virtual impedance.

directly influences the power transfer 
capability of the GFM-ESC, and this magnitude is regulated 
by the reactive power loop and virtual impedance. Therefore,

and virtual impedance settings on the DPTL of the GFM-ESC. A. Control Architecture and Dynamic Model

system. Both the VCL and CCL are implemented using 
proportional–integral (PI) controllers.

exhibits a stronger voltage support capability because it 
employs PCC voltage feedback, whereas droop control 
and LPF-based droop control are based on internal 
potential voltage feedback. Consequently, the VSGbased RPL can achieve a higher DPTL.

conducted with an overload factor of a=1.5. When a 
smaller current limit is adopted, such as a=1.2 or lower,

IV. ADAPTIVE VOLTAGE COMPENSATION STRATEGY FOR 
ENHANCING POWER TRANSFER CAPABILITY OF GFM-ESC 
As demonstrated in Section II, GFM-ESC operating under 
weak or ultra-weak grid conditions often suffer from insufficient 
capacity utilization due to a limited SPTL, particularly under 
charging scenarios. Section III further shows that when the 
dynamic characteristics of the control system are considered, the 
DPTL becomes even lower than the SPTL, making it difficult 
for the converter to operate at the rated power, thereby reducing 
the charging and discharging efficiency of the energy storage 
system. Moreover, this limitation cannot be overcome solely by 
tuning the RPL parameters, such as the voltage regulation 
coefficient kV or the integral gain kQ.

capability and facilitates better utilization of the rated capacity. To address the instability issue of GFM-ESC under ultra-weak

VI. CONCLUSION 
This paper reveals that the GFM-ESC exhibits asymmetry in 
its static power transfer limit (SPTL), where power can be 
delivered in discharging mode but is limited in charging mode. The asymmetry is primarily caused by grid resistance, leading to 
significant power transfer limitations in charging mode under 
weak grid conditions. Regarding the dynamic power transfer 
limit (DPTL), the results show that the DPTL is solely 
determined by the voltage regulation coefficient, while the 
remaining is unaffected by the integral gain and virtual 
impedance. As a result, even when the SPTL is present, 
inadequate dynamic voltage support caused by the voltage 
regulation coefficient can prevent the GFM-ESC from achieving 
rated power output.

I. INTRODUCTION 
HE control stability of converter-based resources has 
become critical to a reliable operation of power systems, 
due to the widespread use of converters in renewable 
power generation, flexible dc or ac power transmission systems, 
and energy-efficient power loads [1], [2]. The stability issues 
have stimulated a significant demand for the grid-forming 
(GFM) capabilities of voltage-source converters (VSCs) [3]. GFM-VSCs typically employs a cascaded control structure 
with distinct timescales and control functionalities [4]. The 
outer control loops, managing the synchronization, power and 
voltage regulation, maintain a nearly constant internal voltage 
phasor in the sub-transient time frame [5]. This is an essential 
specification for GFM-VSCs to deliver instantaneous voltage 
and frequency support [6].

and frequency support [6]. In contrast, the inner control loops, 
such as vector voltage control (VVC) and vector current control 
(VCC), actively shape the output impedance of GFM-VSC, to 
mitigate voltage harmonics [7], limit fault current [8], and to 
dampen the

been widely used, low-frequency resonances are increasingly 
reported on GFM-VSCs under different grid conditions [10]. Recent studies indicate that GFM-VSCs exhibit two typical 
low-frequency resonances in the output power, i.e., the synchronous resonance (SR) [11], [12] and the sub-synchronous

Fig. 1 shows a single-line diagram of a three-phase VSC with

synchronization, the voltage control, and the active power 
regulation of GFM-VSC. The GFM-VSC commonly employs 
the PSC to form its own phase rather than following the vector 
of POC voltage. Different approaches can be used with the PSC, 
e.g., the droop control [34], [35], the virtual synchronous machine (VSM) [36], [37] control, the dc-link voltage control [38],

voltage magnitude of GFM-VSC.

C. Unified GFM and GFL controls 
It is well known that the traditional GFL control has a high 
stability robustness when VSC is connected to stiff grids, yet it 
tends to be unstable with weak grid interconnections [22], [72]. In contrast, the GFM control with the closed-loop VVC shows 
the opposite stability robustness – it furnishes the VSC a higher 
stability robustness under weak grid conditions than operating 
in stiff grids [16], [13]. This duality serves as the motivation to 
unify GFM and GFL controls, taking the best of both to achieve 
high stability robustness against variation of grid strength [73]. Following the control principles, the unified of GFM and GFL 
controls are listed as follows: 
1) Hybrid synchronization and inner loops [28] 
The general idea is to hybridize the traditional GFM and GFL 
control loops.

VII. CONCLUSION 
This paper has given a comprehensive review of the low-frequency issues in GFM-VSC. The root causes of SR and SSR, 
including the origins of oscillation mode and impacts of control 
interactions, have been discussed in detail. It has been pointed 
out that the interactions between outer and inner loops can cause

text:
1. Introduction
With the deep implementation of the “dual carbon” strategic goals, renewable energy
sources such as photovoltaic power are replacing traditional fossil energy at an unprecedented speed [1]. Currently, it is common to combine photovoltaic units and energy storage
to form a photovoltaic-storage system. In this system, when the photovoltaic unit cannot meet the load demand, the energy storage device can be charged and discharged to
maintain the stability of the power supply, improving the flexibility of the system [2,3]. This is because the renewable energy generation units generally cannot provide the crucial
inertia support and damping effect like traditional synchronous generators (SGs) to the
power grid [4]. To address this issue, domestic and foreign scholars have proposed the
concept of grid-forming [3,5,6].

power grid [4]. To address this issue, domestic and foreign scholars have proposed the
concept of grid-forming [3,5,6]. Among them, the VSG is widely used. This control enables
renewable energy to provide J and D to the power grid like traditional synchronous motors,
thereby aligning the relationship between distributed power sources and the power grid

scholars have proposed applying ACL to the VSG strategy [9].

2.2. Photovoltaic-Storage Direct-Current Grid Connection
Traditional photovoltaic and energy storage systems adopt the form of AC grid connection; that is, both the photovoltaic power station and the energy storage station are
connected to the bus through DC/AC converters and then to the power grid. Considering
the influencing factors of the photovoltaic power station and its unpredictable volatility, for
small-power photovoltaic power stations, the mode of DC grid connection for photovoltaic
and energy storage can be considered. In this mode, both the photovoltaic and energy storage are connected through bidirectional DC/DC converters to the same DC/AC converter
and then connected to the power grid [16].

3.2. The Influence of J and D on the Output Characteristics of the VSG
3.2.1. The Influence of J and D on the Active Power Output Characteristics of the VSG
Equation (14) shows that, for a fixed D, raising J lowers the damping ratio, enlarges
overshoot, and stretches both settling time and recovery after any power change; keeping J
constant and increasing D, in contrast, raises the ratio, suppresses overshoot, and shortens
settling time. Hence, J sets the oscillation frequency while D governs how fast the oscillation
dies away.

6. Discussion
6.1. Contrast
This paper proposes an adaptive inertia- and damping-control strategy; when constructing the adaptive functions, the final expressions reported in the manuscript were obtained by simultaneously accounting for multiple constraints and practical considerations—
these include the upper and lower bounds of virtual inertia J and virtual damping D, the
analytical properties of candidate functions (monotonicity, smoothness, and saturation
characteristic), the algorithmic complexity that determines code implementation effort,
and the computational burden as well as total simulation time imposed by the real-time
solver of the used simulation platform. Thereafter, the derived adaptive functions were
embedded into the proposed Grid-Connected Photovoltaic Storage System and tested
under comprehensive disturbance scenarios.

paper_title: Optimal Operation of Grid-Forming-Controlled PV and Energy Storage Converters in Low-Voltage Distribution Networks
text:
1. Introduction
The construction of a renewable energy source (RES)-dominated power system is essential for fulfilling climate commitments and accelerating the green energy transition [1,2]. Nevertheless, the high penetration of intermittent RESs, along with the proliferation of
power electronic devices, poses new challenges to loads, active distribution networks
(DNs), and the power system as a whole [3]. For example, the integration of numerous
photovoltaic (PV) panels via grid-following (GFL) control-based converters can cause a
voltage rise at the point of common coupling (PCC) and output power limitation in severe
cases [4]. In response, the integration of inductive power–electronic loads results in a low
power factor and harmonics at the PCC, thereby affecting system efficiency [5].

paper_title: Optimal Operation of Grid-Forming-Controlled PV and Energy Storage Converters in Low-Voltage Distribution Networks
text:

power factor and harmonics at the PCC, thereby affecting system efficiency [5]. Due to
the ability to support voltage and frequency, grid-forming control (GFM)-based converters have been increasingly applied in both the main grid and DNs [6,7]. Owing to the
stable voltage-source characteristics, GFM-based converters offer better adaptability in
low-voltage DNs (LVDNs) than GFL-based converters and present a novel perspective for
tackling complex power quality (PQ) and RES utilization issues. Energies 2026, 19, 3647

Existing research on GFM-based converters has primarily focused on control strategies. Due to the ability to provide inertia, damping, and frequency–voltage characteristics
by simulating synchronous generators [8,9], droop control and virtual synchronous generator (VSG) control have been widely used. In recent years, nonlinear GFM schemes
(including matching control and virtual oscillator control) have emerged as alternative
approaches [10,11]. However, these GFM methods primarily focus on providing frequency
and voltage support for the main grid. Consequently, the aforementioned GFM schemes
neglect comprehensive PQ management in LVDNs, leading to fragmented research that
targets individual issues rather than holistic optimization. To address specific PQ problems in LVDNs, many GFM-based strategies have been proposed.

In [12], an adaptive dynamic voltage support scheme for multiple GFM-based converters is proposed, which enables distributed, communication-free coordination through
local parameter estimation to maximize voltage support efficiency. To mitigate harmonic
distortion in weak grids, Tarraso et al. [13] proposed a selective harmonic compensation
scheme for GFM-based converters, which uses virtual admittance branches to suppress
specific harmonics and naturally shares the mitigation effort among parallel converters,
effectively reducing THD at the PCC.

effectively reducing THD at the PCC. Reactive power sharing among multiple GFM-based
converters is another critical concern, since mismatches in line impedance or converter
parameters may result in uneven power distribution and circulating currents. To address
this issue, a feed-forward droop control with line impedance compensation is proposed
in [14], which tracks line impedance online and compensates voltage drops in the dq
frame. This approach effectively eliminates the adverse effects of impedance mismatches,
achieving precise reactive power sharing and circulating current suppression without prior
knowledge of line parameters.

in [15] further addresses the trade-off between sharing accuracy and system damping
by adjusting the reactive droop coefficient in real time, while remaining applicable to
grids with unknown R/X ratios. However, most of the above studies adopt control-level
strategies, which are insufficient for complex PQ issues. In essence, this complex PQ and RES utilization issue constitutes a multi-objective
optimization operation problem, which has been explored by some researchers from
this perspective.

text:

optimization operation problem, which has been explored by some researchers from
this perspective. In [16], a hybrid HGPC (combining Grey Wolf Optimization (GWO),
Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), and Cuckoo Search Optimization (CO))-based multiobjective approach is proposed for joint EV charging station and capacitor placement,
balancing traffic flow capture, power loss, and voltage deviation in a DN. In [17], Nazih et al.
employed a multi-objective whale optimization algorithm (WOA) to maximize distributed
generator (DG) hosting capacity while reducing loss and voltage unbalance in unbalanced
DNs. In [18], the Non-Dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) is adopted
for multi-objective coordination of ESSs in DC DNs, effectively minimizing operational
costs and energy losses.

3. Simplified Multi-Objective Optimization Problem
The optimization problem described in (16) and (17) is inherently multi-objective in
nature, meaning that its solution comprises a Pareto front rather than a unique optimum. Consequently, a preference-based selection step is required before the final decision can be
implemented, and this step imposes a considerable additional computational cost. Thus,
the multi-objective optimization problem in (16) and (17) is not easy to solve in real time. To facilitate real-time implementation, this study proposes a hierarchical multiobjective optimization scheme that converts the original multi-objective problem in (16)
and (17) into sequential single-objective ones according to the priority of each objective.

paper_title: Optimal Operation of Grid-Forming-Controlled PV and Energy Storage Converters in Low-Voltage Distribution Networks
text:
that converts the original multi-objective problem in (16)
and (17) into sequential single-objective ones according to the priority of each objective. The prioritization is established as follows: (1) the highest priority is given to minimizing
voltage deviation, as secure and reliable voltage supply is the foremost guarantee for
end-users; (2) the second priority is assigned to maximizing PV power generation, so
that users can reap maximum economic benefits once voltage security is ensured; (3) the
lowest priority is given to minimizing system power losses, as they are directly linked to
operational costs. This hierarchical approach does not pursue global Pareto optimality but
rather an engineering-feasible compromised optimum, where higher-priority objectives
are strictly satisfied at the possible expense of lower-priority ones.

4.2. Improved PSO Algorithm
According to (24), the velocity update of traditional PSO particles relies on random
numbers r1 and r2, which leads to slow convergence and difficulty in escaping local optima. To address this issue, an improved PSO is proposed, where all random numbers are replaced
by chaotic sequences.

5. Simulation Verification
This section validates the effectiveness and rationality of the proposed optimal operation
strategy in the simulations. The electrical and control parameters used in the simulations are
shown as Table 2. In addition, the GFM-based converter adopts droop control.
Furthermore, the parameters of the proposed PSO are selected within commonly used
ranges, with their specific values determined through offline tests. The Lorenz system
adopts its classical parameters, striking a balance between preserving chaotic dynamics and
computational efficiency. The normalization strategy employs linear mapping to unify all
decision variables to the same order of magnitude, thereby preventing any single dimension
from dominating the particle update process.

6. Controller Hardware-in-the-Loop Experimental Validation
To validate the real-time execution capability of the proposed strategy, a Controller
Hardware-in-the-Loop (CHIL) platform is established, as shown in Figure 14. The LVDN
physical power stage is emulated in the Modelingtech MT 6090 simulator, manufactured by
Shanghai Yuankuan Energy Technology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China), with a 1µs time step for
high-fidelity transient reproduction. The control sampling period and the PWM switching
frequency are both set to 10 kHz (i.e., 100 µs). By calculation, the worst-case execution
time of the underlying GFM control loop—including measurement, communication, and
controller update—is estimated to be approximately 85 µs, which is well within the 100 µs
control interval, leaving a 15 µs safety margin.

is not executed in every control cycle; it is triggered only upon significant disturbances (grid
voltage fluctuations, load changes, or PV variations). The measured execution time for a
full PSO optimization is approximately 20 ms, which is acceptable for disturbance-response
scenarios, as typical grid disturbances evolve on a time scale of hundreds of milliseconds to
seconds. In steady-state operation, the system relies on previously computed optimal setpoints to avoid unnecessary computational overhead. For future hardware implementation,
we plan to adopt FPGA-based acceleration to further reduce the PSO computation latency
and enhance overall real-time performance.

text:
7. Conclusions
In this study, an improved PSO-algorithm-based hierarchical optimal operation strategy is proposed for LVDNs integrated with GFM-based PV and ESSs. The proposed
strategy can simultaneously address voltage fluctuations, low penetration of RES, and
high system power losses, and it is convenient for real-time implementation. The main
conclusions are as follows:
(1)
A priority-based hierarchical simplification method is designed to enable real-time
control feasibility, which transforms the multi-objective optimization problem into
single ones. The comparative analysis of optimization results verifies the effectiveness
of the proposed optimization strategy in reducing load voltage deviation and system
power losses.

paper_title: Optimal Operation of Grid-Forming-Controlled PV and Energy Storage Converters in Low-Voltage Distribution Networks
text:

of the proposed optimization strategy in reducing load voltage deviation and system
power losses. (2)
Compared with traditional algorithms (NSGA-II, GA, and PSO), the improved PSO
algorithm exhibits better performance: reducing total convergence time by 36.9%
while achieving an optimal power loss of 0.5950 kW. (3)
The proposed strategy is verified to support reliable operation in both grid-connected
and off-grid modes, maintaining the PCC voltage within 0.90–1.07 p.u. and frequency
within 49.8–50.2 Hz under all test conditions. Future work will extend the proposed strategy to multi-GFM-based converters in parallel operation, refine the system loss model, and develop high-dimensional optimization
methods for complex LVDNs to address scalability challenges in coordinating multiple
DGs.
